extracted_by: hand, T-0294 — the Democrat read, December 1834
note: Vol. II No. 4, the last number of the month and the year. Page 3 column 5 is the only Tesseract fallback in the issue and it is the single most legible column of the whole month — one physical column, full sentences — and it carries the month's legal business: two estates administered, a chancery order returnable at the Court House at Chicago, and an auction of a dead man's stock and furniture at Bates' Auction Room on the last Wednesday of the year. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST OF ANY OFFICE STANDS IN THIS ISSUE.

Twice-weekly auctions are a quantity of street activity a reconstruction can actually stage. THE PLACEMENT ANCHOR IS CARRIED OVER FROM THE 17 DECEMBER PRINTING and its offset text is quoted from there, because this setting keeps the street and loses “near the bridge”; recording the business twice with the same anchor is what makes the two printings one storefront in the gazetteer rather than two. Garrett's is the only NEW Chicago storefront the month announces.

claims.notes: THE LIBRARY THE TOWN VOTED FOR IN NOVEMBER IS COLLECTING BOOKS BY CHRISTMAS, AND IT HAS AN ADDRESS. T-0293 read the founding call at 1834-11-26 c001 — a meeting of citizens favourable to the establishment of a Library and Reading Room, at the Presbyterian church, on Thursday 27 November — and the notice here is what came of it four weeks later: a committee, a purchasing plan, and a drop-off point at Messrs. Jones & King's office on south water street, entrance first door north of something the column cut away. So the Lyceum's library begins life inside a hardware merchant's counting room, and Jones & King's office gets a documented street and a documented door — the only placement evidence this corpus carries for that firm. The clause is set in two woven half-columns here and the unshuffling is stated in `normalized`; the 1834-12-17 printing (page 3 column 2) is the worse witness and is not claimed.

claims.notes: A DATED, TIMED, PLACED EVENT — ten o'clock on the morning of Wednesday 31 December 1834, at Bates' Auction Room in Chicago — which is the kind of thing a walkable reconstruction can actually stage. It also names a room the gazetteer did not have: BATES' AUCTION ROOM, distinct from David Carver's auction and commission store on South Water street (1834-12-03 c010's neighbour on page 4) and from A. Garrett's new store near the bridge (c001), so Chicago supports THREE auction rooms in December 1834. J. Bates jr. already stands in the gazetteer with an auction store anchored on “the Street leading from the draw-bridge to the oak woods and Blue Island”; this notice does not repeat that placement and none is asserted here. Six months' credit on anything over five dollars is the issue's clearest statement of how little cash the town had.

claims.notes: DAVID LAUGHTON IS DEAD BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, AND THE PAPER SAYS SO IN PLAIN PROBATE LANGUAGE. The Laughtons kept the tavern and trading house on the Des Plaines west of the town, on the road every traveller from the south and west came in on; a reconstruction of July 1835 that puts him behind that bar would be putting a dead man there. This is exactly the class of fact the epic exists to catch — not a new building, but a correction to who was alive in the scene — and it is documented, dated 1 December 1834, and administered by the county rather than by a family, which is itself a fact about the household. The second printing of the same notice stands at 1834-12-03 page 3 column 2 in a badly interleaved column; this is the legible witness.

claims.notes: THE COURT HOUSE AT CHICAGO IS NAMED AS THE PLACE THE NEXT TERM WILL BE HOLDEN, ON 14 MAY 1835 — six weeks before the scene date — SO THERE IS A COURT HOUSE, and the county's own order says so. That is a public building this reconstruction has to account for. The order carries a second fact about the town, and it is a poorer one: the Clerk seals it with his PRIVATE seal, “no seal of office being provided”, so Cook county in December 1834 has a court house and no county seal. It also documents the Democrat's legal-notice business — four weeks' publication, first insertion within sixty days — which is a large part of what kept the paper alive. The date is read as the 8th where the transcription sets “Sth”; the column is cut at its right edge throughout and the fragments of the neighbouring column are quoted with the lines, which is why the quote carries stray letters the normalized reading does not.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S DEBT-COLLECTION MACHINERY, NAMED. Clybourn's threat is to put his paper in the hands of “Collins” after 10 January, and the gazetteer already carries Collins & Caton, attorneys and counsellors at law and solicitors in chancery, up stairs on South Water street. The surname alone is what is printed, so the person minted is “Collins” and NOT the firm; joining them would need a stated merge rule, and the whole-name key means the two cannot coalesce by accident. Read beside the Bates' auction notice's six months' credit (c004) and the two cautions against purchasing notes (1834-12-03 c010, 1834-12-10's Sweet notice at c010 here) it is the same picture from three sides: almost nothing in Chicago in December 1834 is paid for in cash.

claims.notes: THE THIRD ESTRAY OF THE MONTH AFTER WENTWORTH'S OXEN (1834-12-10 c003) AND THE CLYBOURN NOTICES, AND ALL OF THEM ARE PENNED IN NOVEMBER. Loose cattle in the last weeks before hard frost is a seasonal fact rather than a set of separate accidents: the harvest is off, fences are down, and animals drift. Three separate freeholders print notices about it in four issues, which for a town this size means loose stock was a normal winter condition of the streets and the prairie edge — something a reconstruction of the scene should not leave empty.

claims.notes:
THE SECOND WITNESS TO THE BUILDING CLAIMED AT 1834-12-17 c006, AND IT READS THE LOT NUMBER DIFFERENTLY. Here it is Lot 2; a week earlier it is Lot 9. Both printings are Vision-set and neither is the obviously better reading, so BOTH are claimed, each quoting its own digit, and neither is amended to agree with the other — an agreement manufactured between two transcriptions is not evidence. Block 1 on North Water street is common to both, and that much is safe. The page images settle the digit in one look and this run files the ticket for it.

AMENDED BY T-0328 on 2026-08-29, AND THE QUOTE IS UNTOUCHED. The question this note left open — which digit the page carries — is answered by three further printings of the same standing advertisement that neither this read nor the November read had claimed: 1834-11-26 page 3 column 3 (c010), 1834-12-03 page 3 column 3 (c025) and 1834-12-10 page 3 column 3 (c012). All three set `Lot 2`, as does 1834-12-24 c012. FOUR PRINTINGS TO ONE, and they are four separate settings of the type rather than one reading repeated. THE READING IS LOT 2, block 1, North Water street. This is not an agreement manufactured between two transcriptions — which is what T-0294 rightly refused — it is a majority of independent witnesses, and no transcription was edited to produce it. It is still a transcription read and not a scan read: the page images would make it `scan_verified`, and they are not in the repository, so both claims stay `transcription_mediated`.

THIS IS THE COLUMN THAT WINS, and it wins on company rather than on its own authority.
